---
title: "Quiz: level sets and marching squares"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A grid point is above when $I > c$; cell corners 0, 1, 2, 3 = top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left; case index $= \sum 2^k$ over the corners above $c$.

---

**Q1.** What is the difference between thresholding an image at $c$ and computing its level set at $c$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One produces pixels, the other a curve.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Thresholding labels each pixel above or below $c$: a region made of whole pixels. The level set $\{I = c\}$ is the boundary between those regions, a curve that passes between pixel centres at the interpolated position, with sub-pixel precision.
:::

---

**Q2.** A cell has corners (top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left) = 2, 7, 8, 1 and $c = 5$. What is its case index, and which edges are crossed?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which corners are above 5?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Corners 1 and 2 are above: case $2 + 4 = 6$. The crossed edges are the top edge (2 → 7) and the bottom edge (8 → 1); the contour runs from top to bottom, like a vertical line.
:::

---

**Q3.** On an edge from 30 to 90, where is the crossing for $c = 45$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$t = (c - I_a)/(I_b - I_a)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$t = 15/60 = 0.25$: a quarter of the way from the corner with 30.
:::

---

**Q4.** Why do the line segments of neighbouring cells always join up, although each cell is handled on its own?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What do the two cells have in common?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
They share the edge between them, with the same two corner values: both find the same crossing point (or both find none). So every segment ending on that edge meets the segment of the neighbour there.
:::

---

**Q5.** Which cases are ambiguous, and what are the two possible contours?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Look for diagonal corners.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Cases 5 and 10: two diagonal corners above, the other two below. The contour can **separate** the two bright corners (each cut off on its own) or **join** them (the two dark corners cut off instead). Both choices give closed curves; they differ in topology.
:::

---

**Q6.** A saddle cell has corners 6, 2, 6, 2 (clockwise from top-left) and $c = 4$. What does the asymptotic decider do?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$f^\ast = (I_0 I_2 - I_1 I_3)/(I_0 + I_2 - I_1 - I_3)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$f^\ast = (36 - 4)/(12 - 4) = 32/8 = 4 = c$: exactly the borderline (with the rule "join if $f^\ast > c$" it separates). Any change of a value tips the decision. This is the case where the bilinear interpolant's level curve at $c$ is a pair of crossing lines.
:::

---

**Q7.** A noisy image gives 300 contours at $c$ where you expect 5 objects. Name two things you could do, and their side effects.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Change the image, or filter the result.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Blur before extracting (fewer and smoother contours; but small objects shrink and thin necks break), or discard contours enclosing less than a minimum area (keeps the shapes; but real small objects go too, and the remaining boundaries stay ragged). Choosing $c$ further from the noise level also helps.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show with the shoelace formula that the triangle $(0, 0), (4, 0), (0, 3)$ has area 6, and that listing its corners in the opposite order gives $-6$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$A = \tfrac12\sum(x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Terms: $(0 \cdot 0 - 4 \cdot 0) + (4 \cdot 3 - 0 \cdot 0) + (0 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 3) = 12$, so $A = 6$. Reversed, $(0,0), (0,3), (4,0)$: $(0 - 0) + (0 \cdot 0 - 4 \cdot 3) + (0 - 0) = -12$, $A = -6$.
:::
